source.title: Prefix Guidance: A Steering Wheel for Large Language Models to Defend Against Jailbreak Attacks
source.authors: Jia-Wei Zhao; Kejiang Chen; Xiaojian Yuan; Wei-Ming Zhang

record.file_problem: The full paper is present and usable. Some text and tables have OCR/flattening artifacts, particularly the Guanaco appendix table.
record.tranche_reason: It evaluates whether jailbreak attacks elicit harmful outputs from chat models, including GCG, which the paper describes as using suffixes to target affirmative openings. This is a behavioral test of one part of V4, not a reproduction of the original fine-tuning or KL-divergence measurements.
record.gate_note: The paper states that the first few output tokens influence generation and cites prior work on forced prefixes; those cited findings are not this study's results. Its own measured attack outcomes without a defense are recorded below. Prefix Guidance and other defense results are omitted: they report the performance of the paper's defense method, not whether a compliant opening bypasses safety.
record.test_reason: This is a defense paper (Prefix Guidance). Its only results bearing on the claim are the no-defense baselines for GCG, a suffix attack optimised toward affirmative openings, on three 7B chat models (Table 2, Table 5). Those numbers measure whether suffixes defeat refusal, which is part of V4. AutoDAN, PAIR, DeepInception and ReNeLLM are prompt-level or template jailbreaks that the paper does not tie to the opening tokens, so their rows are not V4 evidence. The PG results come from the paper's own method.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is essentially right. PG is reported comparable to or better than SafeDecoding at reducing ASR and harm scores across three models and five attacks. Capability loss is 0–5%: about 4% on Vicuna and 5% on Guanaco, with a 1% gain on Llama2. The authors make no claim about why safety is shallow; they cite first-token influence (GCG, forced prefixes) only as motivation.
record.recipe_differences: The study evaluates jailbreak attacks and proposes a refusal-prefix defense; it does not apply the original harmful/benign fine-tuning or aligned-versus-base KL methods. The attack prompts for several methods are drawn from prior repositories.
record.method_sensitivity: Attack success varies substantially by model and attack method; Llama2-7B-Chat has much lower no-defense ASR than Vicuna-7B-v1.5 and Guanaco-7B for several attacks.

fits_no_version.finding: Prefilling a refusal opening (e.g. "I'm sorry, but I cannot") and classifying the continuation cut jailbreak ASR to near 0% for most attacks. ReNeLLM on Vicuna is the exception, staying at 54%. This is the defense's own performance and is not catalogued as rows.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Forcing a refusal-style opening steers aligned chat models toward refusal and harm recognition across jailbreak types: the mirror image of V4.

record.problems: No uncertainty estimates are reported. ASR is determined by refusal-phrase matching, which may not precisely identify harmful compliance; the authors acknowledge this and also report a GPT4o-mini harmfulness score. The Guanaco appendix table is flattened in the supplied text.
record.rows_left_out: No rows omitted under the 60-row limit. Prefix Guidance and other defense-method outcomes are not catalogued because they report the performance of the paper's proposed defense rather than a compliant-opening bypass test.

untested.parts: Prefilling a compliant start; decoding changes. There is no no-attack control, and nothing isolates whether GCG works by shifting the opening tokens.
All; no deepening training. PG is an inference-time refusal prefix plus a classifier.

record.verdict_notes: V4 evidence is limited to the GCG no-defense baselines. These prompts were reused from the SafeDecoding repository rather than generated by the study. ASR uses refusal-keyword matching. No unattacked baseline is reported, so attack-attributable compliance cannot be separated from base compliance, especially for Vicuna and Guanaco, which have weak safety tuning. The record's 'challenges' label (ReNeLLM on Llama2) is removed: ReNeLLM is not an opening-based attack and its prompts were transferred from Claude2.

versions.untested_parts: No fine-tuning on harmful examples or measurement of refusal after such fine-tuning.
No fine-tuning on benign instruction data or measurement of its effect on harmful compliance.
Evaluates attack methods, including GCG; does not test compliant-token prefilling or decoding changes, and does not isolate whether an opening-token change causes the attack success.
No weight or rank localization test.
No test of why safety behaviour is shallow.
No training to deepen safety or evaluation of whether deepening holds up.

relationships.condition: GCG suffix attack, no defense, Vicuna-7B-v1.5 and Guanaco-7B
relationships.reason: GCG ASR is 98% on both models, with harm scores of 4.50 and 4.28 (A1, A2, A21, A22). No no-attack baseline is reported.
relationships.display_finding: GCG reached 98% attack success on both models with harm scores of 4.50 and 4.28, and no no-attack baseline was reported.

relationships.condition: GCG suffix attack, no defense, Llama2-7B-Chat
relationships.reason: On the more strongly safety-tuned Llama2, GCG reaches only 30% ASR with a harm score of 2.58 (A11, A12).
relationships.display_finding: GCG reached only 30% attack success, with a harm score of 2.58, on the strongly safety-tuned Llama2.
